title: The Calm Before the Storm
desc:
The sky outside the command center was overcast, about to rain. Yazov turned over, trying to close his eyes, but today again he couldn't sleep. His personal doctor had been protesting for several days, hoping he would get some proper rest. Yazov himself knew that he could not fall before the Great Trial arrived. He was now the helmsman of this raging war machine that was Russia. If he were to fall, it was uncertain whether the country's last path to salvation could continue in the direction he had envisioned.

A profound cold suddenly welled up in Yazov's heart. For the Great Trial, he and everyone he trusted had used various methods, from propaganda to violence, to urge, even force, the Russian people to submit to the cause of the Great Trial. He had known for years that both he and the people he trusted were just parts of this war machine of the Great Trial. They had already filled it with fuel. At this point, the Great Trial was unstoppable.

But what if we fail?

Yazov couldn't help but think of the previous discussions: the Nazi nuclear weapons completely destroying the League's leadership, the final nuclear exchange failing to launch; the Black League's soldiers failing to resist the Nazis, the Great Trial being stillborn from the start; information leaking, the American and Japanese degenerates and the Nazis forming a joint army and setting foot on Russian soil...

He suddenly felt a stomach ache. The people of Russia had already endured countless sacrifices for the Great Trial, but what if all their efforts and sacrifices were in vain?

title: Returning to the Fold
desc:
He slipped out while the guards weren't looking, not even fully dressed. The clouds were still dark, flashes of lightning streaking through them with increasing frequency, but the thunder was intermittent. He walked aimlessly. Over a dozen years had passed, and Omsk had changed a lot. The crude buildings of the past had long been razed, replaced by a part of the final bastion for the Great Trial. He suddenly felt a bit tired and looked up. This was the training ground. Just this morning, he had been here, addressing a new batch of soldiers. Those young men's eyes were filled with fanaticism and confidence, as if they could overcome any difficulty, just like he had been a dozen years ago.

He was a bit tired, and randomly found a chair, sitting on one side, leaving the other for someone who would never return—Karbyshev. The wind began to rise, and a light, drizzling rain began to fall on the earth, and on Yazov's body, which brought him a strange sense of tranquility. He looked into the distance. Young soldiers were conducting cross-country training under the command of their officers. Although these new recruits ran in a crooked line, under the leadership of their officers, not a single one fell behind. Yazov nodded. This was exactly the role of an officer. He could lead the tender new recruits to learn from scratch, to clarify their responsibilities within the collective. With them, the young people could grow the fastest and be competent for their duties.

A howling cold wind accompanied a heavy downpour, and rolling thunder echoed across the land. The training队伍们 (duìwumen - teams) ran back to their barracks in an orderly fashion. Yazov's heart, however, felt lighter. Just as the old general had said in his last speech, personal desire must never be placed above the needs of the people, and he was the same.

Looking back on the path he had traveled, he had walked a journey of blood and fire: from Tara to Sverdlovsk, from Samara to Irkutsk. A strong, unified Russia was now built. As the navigator of the League, he had already pointed Russia in the right direction. In the past, the old general had been his mentor, guiding him to understand the true meaning of the Great Trial. And today, at the crossroads just before the Great Trial, to evade responsibility, to choose to retreat, would not only be a betrayal of the ultimate truth of the Great Trial, but also a betrayal of all the Russian people, and betrayal is unforgivable.

A group of guards and an aide quickly ran to Yazov's side, draping a coat over him and holding up an umbrella. “It's time to go back. Comrade Savintsev and the others are waiting for your next instructions.”

title: Two Swords, One Purpose
desc:
Vladimir Kryuchkov stared at Nikolai Shchelokov, who was similarly sizing him up across the table.

This was a meeting between the intelligence bureau and the statistics bureau. Though just a meeting, the seasoned intuition of both men told them this was something big.

“The Commander-in-Chief has ordered a more detailed and clear observation of the Teutonic German barbarians' civilian intelligence. I'm sure you know this is a very important matter. It's common knowledge within the League that you are a genius in this field,” Kryuchkov began, stating his purpose.

“Oh, of course. For the smooth progress of the Great Trial, to crush those fascist scoundrels, how could I not follow the Commander-in-Chief's command? I am of course very familiar with civilian statistics. Every reassuring number on the League's statistical tables is the result of my meticulous work. I certainly wouldn't refuse the dry, nauseating characters of the Teutonic dregs,” Shchelokov smiled slightly, showing his steadfastness to the operative across from him.

“I'm not surprised by that answer. What I want to know more is how you view the new product of the merger between the statistics bureau and the intelligence bureau---the League European Security Bureau. This is the new agency facing the largest tasks the League currently has. I wonder how much spare capacity you have,” Kryuchkov's expression turned solemn as he took a step forward.

Shchelokov's expression grew serious. “The League's tasks in the preparatory stage of the war are very heavy. Precise statistical calculations require a lot of time and energy. I currently work 14 hours a day, and sometimes work overtime. My capacity is currently limited.”

Hearing this, Kryuchkov's brow furrowed, his eyes dimming with a hint of disappointment.

Until Shchelokov's next words.

“But if it means delivering a powerful blow to those bastards who tore the flesh from Mother Russia, I will lead all the intelligence operatives to work one more hour, and add two more days of overtime a week.” “As long as it allows the Great Trial to proceed smoothly!” Shchelokov stood up and firmly extended his hand to Kryuchkov.

Kryuchkov's face cleared, and he also stood up, extending his hand to Shchelokov.

The meeting of their two hands was not just the expansion of a department, not just an agreement between two operatives.

options.name: “It was the League taking one step closer to successful revenge.”
options.text: “It was the League taking one step closer to successful revenge.”

title: Demolition
desc:
“Old Valery, let's go! Those black-clothed men are unreasonable! You should sign the contract, the amount those operatives are offering isn't small. If you don't sign, they said they'll resort to extreme measures.”

“I'm not signing! This is my home! My family has lived here for generations. Even Bukharin didn't touch my home. I'm staying here. Unless they step over my dead body, I will never leave!”

“Fine, you stay here. We're leaving.”

Old Valery watched his neighbors turn and leave in frustration. He closed the door, a cold sneer on his lips: “So clueless. When dealing with the government, isn't it all about making a scene to get more?”

He went to the kitchen, took out two bottles of vodka from the cabinet, and chugged them down, his courage growing. As a man who had read a few books, old Valery had always looked down on his neighbors. In his impression, they were vulgar, uncultured, and blindly obedient. When Bukharin was still around, these people would do whatever the Soviet government said. But old Valery was different. He had a brain. He would protest, he would fight for more, he would cry in front of those Soviet officials in public. After a good cry, the Soviet officials wouldn't dare threaten him anymore and would obediently deliver rice and white flour to his door.

He propped his legs up on a chair, about to take a nap. The sound of footsteps and a huge roar grew closer and closer, making old Valery increasingly irritated. These dogs of the government wouldn't even let him sleep today!

He angrily walked to the window, intending to yell at them. A black-clothed man with glasses was still talking to the one in charge standing next to the bulldozer. “Hey, listen up, you're not tearing down my house, I will never agree!”

The leading officer laughed. “Did you all hear that? This house is obstructing the Great Trial project, defying government decrees. Now, correct this error immediately. Begin construction!”

The moment the rumbling bulldozer started moving forward, old Valery sobered up. He screamed, wanting to escape, but there was no time. The moment the bulldozer reached him, a question suddenly came to his mind: “Didn't these people shout about being for the people of Russia? Why is the only thing left for him now death?”

title: A Friendly Activity
desc:
“A vivid and enticing lobbying effort. Your performance has indeed exceeded our expectations, Mr. Peter.”

Expert Butler took a sip of his coffee, smiled at Peter before him, and then picked up a document. In the past few days, the American Council on Foreign Relations had begun to pay attention to this group of Russians who had traveled thousands of miles to America and were spending money like water. Through FBI intelligence and information provided by government officials within the council, they had confirmed that these Russians had been seeking various connections inside and outside the government, with think tanks, experts, and retired military personnel. They hoped the US government could provide economic and military support to the new Russian government to counter a possible Nazi invasion. They had successfully lobbied a retired lieutenant general to publicly support Russia yesterday, and today, they had come to the Council on Foreign Relations.

“Lobbying alone is not enough to persuade the US government to support you,” another expert said. “I'm sure you know that our America is a free country, and every American has their own ideas and lives. You want the US government to support you against the Nazis, but the American people may think that the Nazis will retaliate against us, and thus refuse to provide you with sufficient support.”

“Moreover, in the propaganda of previous years, we can clearly see that you previously claimed to be establishing a democratic and free government. Your official documents promised to hold free elections in Russia. But to this day, your Russian Rejuvenation Government has not held a public election, which clearly violates your promise.”

“So, this requires you gentlemen to come forward and explain to the various classes of America, to tell them that we Russians are your best friends, and the forefront of resistance against the Nazis. Only the brightest minds like you can ensure US-Russian friendship,” Peter said unhurriedly.

“But we in America can choose not to support you, just like decades ago. The Nazis cannot reach our homeland.”

“It's different now, sir,” Peter said. “According to intelligence obtained by our government, Nazi Germany is attempting a new round of expansion. They are using the pretext of countering us to expand their Reichskommissariats in the Russian region. Once the Nazis successfully expand eastward, the entire Arctic region will be completely controlled by the Nazis, which will greatly threaten America's Arctic and Pacific interests.”

The experts looked at each other and nodded. It was Butler who spoke up again: “Sir, what kind of effort do you hope we will make?”

Peter took out a few checks and a document from his briefcase. “This is a small token of the Russian people's sincerity. We sincerely hope that the American people will sympathize with and support us. This is the result of our lobbying of Mr. Stanley Hoffmann. He has agreed to support the just cause of the Russian people.”

A few days later, the new issue of the American magazine *Foreign Affairs* published an essay titled 'On the Balance of Power.'

title: The Two-Faced Man
desc:
Guderianstadt, inside the government building. Despite the group of black-clothed madmen on the border, and the busy local settlers and defense forces, the officials within the government were quite optimistic. After all, what could a bunch of losers from over 20 years ago possibly do?

“Sir, help us, you don't know, those Georgians are simply lawless. Every Wednesday, they gather in droves and riot in our Russian communities, vandalizing our shops. They don't care about the government's laws at all!” a one-eyed Russian in tattered clothes pleaded tearfully to the German official before him.

“No, no, no, Mr. Viktor, I must be clear, the conflicts of your inferior races are none of our concern.” The German official tilted his head back, crossed his arms, and looked down his nose at the Russian before him. “The law of the Greater Germanic Reich has stipulated that we have a policy of preferential treatment for the peoples of the Caucasus region. The reason they are causing trouble, I imagine, is that you Russians must have done something wrong to anger these Caucasians, which is why they are retaliating against you like this.”

“But, but we are a part of the Reichskommissariat after all. We also pay taxes to you sirs, we, we…” The Russian man's head hung even lower, his eyes not daring to look at the German official, just staring at the desk full of documents, sobbing uncontrollably.

The official, annoyed by his crying, waved his hand dismissively. “Get out, a coward of an inferior race. Don't come bothering us!”

Viktor walked back to his community, dejected. A group of Russians quickly surrounded him. “Viktor, did the German sirs agree to help us drive away those damn Georgians?”

“No, they said we are weak and not worthy of their help. We can only rely on ourselves.”

Amidst the surprised and angry arguments of the Russians, Viktor walked back to his home. As soon as the door closed, the pain on his face vanished, replaced by a cold, steely resolve. He quickly ran to a desk, took out a prepared pen and paper, and began to write down every Nazi official's name he could remember from memory.

Viktor walked back to his community, dejected. A group of Russians quickly surrounded him. “Viktor, did the German sirs agree to help us drive away those damn Georgians?”

“No, they said we are weak and not worthy of their help. We can only rely on ourselves.”

Amidst the surprised and angry arguments of the Russians, Viktor walked back to his home. As soon as the door closed, the pain on his face vanished, replaced by a cold, steely resolve. He quickly ran to a desk, took out a prepared pen and paper, and began to write down every Nazi official's name he could remember from memory.

title: Malicious Competition
desc:
“Pah, a bunch of inferior races. If you don't have the money, don't even try to compete. Insisting on babbling on and on, trying to snatch things from us, engaging in malicious bidding. If you don't have money, you should just honestly buy the lower-grade goods. Trying to compete with us for the best! They don't have the strength!” Walther stood on the deck of the ocean liner, venting his frustrations to his friend.

“On the bright side, we still got the goods, didn't we?” his friend Schulte smiled at him. “These CNC machine tools made in Guangdong are all good stuff. The country's been shouting about some technological innovation for years, and after all this time, they still haven't produced anything of such high quality. We bought such high-quality goods on our first trip. We'll definitely be able to sell them for a sky-high price when we get back.”

“True. Let's not talk about it anymore. I'm a bit tired, I'm going to go get some sleep. Arguing with those damn inferior races just ruins my good mood. This trip still has a few months of sea travel. Sigh, can't the Italians be a bit smarter? Insisting on charging such high passage fees, forcing us to go around the Cape of Good Hope, adding so much extra cost.”

“Don't think about it, my friend. Go get your sleep.”

Walther said no more. He slowly walked back to his luxurious private cabin. Lying on the bed, he began to think about his wonderful future: these goods, as representatives of high-end manufacturing, were always priceless in the country. The big corporations would surely pay a fortune to acquire them. With this money, he would ask his uncle to get him a public office. After a few years, he wouldn't have to run errands himself anymore.

Just as he was lost in thought, a muffled thud suddenly came from the side of the ship, followed by a loud bang. The whole ship shook violently. Walther was thrown to the floor. He scrambled to his feet. A few crew members opened the cabin door and found him.

“Mr. Walther, our ship has sustained serious damage. The right side of the hull is already severely listing. The ship is not going to make it. You must escape with us now.”

“No! What about our cargo? This cargo is the precious property of the Greater Germanic Reich! To just abandon it is a betrayal of the Greater Germanic Reich! Quick, take these things with us!”

Several crew members directly carried Walther out. “I'm sorry, sir, we were only ordered to protect your life. Those machines are too heavy, the lifeboats can't carry them. You'll have to think of another way.”

title: An Unwilling Appointment
desc:
Lorenz stared blankly at the few black-clothed men before him. He still couldn't figure out what had happened. Just a few days ago, he was vacationing on a beach in Lisbon. On his way home, everything suddenly went black. Then, he was in a pitch-black room for several months. During these months, the only person he could see was the guard who brought him food every day. He had tried to shout and scream more than once, hoping someone would notice him, but even after clapping his hands until they were red, no one came to see him. Over time, Lorenz himself gave up struggling, spending his days either eating or sleeping. He even felt like he had gained a few pounds.

After an unknown number of days, someone finally came. It was a few black-clothed men. They took Lorenz out of the dark room, put a black hood over his head. For the rest of the journey, Lorenz could only rely on his senses. He felt like he was being led by these black-clothed men into a car, followed by a long journey. The road was not good, bumpy all the way. He gradually gave up thinking. He only knew that when they finally took off the hood, he was here.

“Hello, Mr. Lorenz,” one of the black-clothed men broke the silence. “I am Black League Operative 520321. You may not know me, just call me Ivan.”

Lorenz's dormant brain finally began to function again. After a moment, he asked the man before him with a question: “Are you… Russians?”

“Strictly speaking, we are the Russian Rejuvenation Government,” Ivan politely explained. “Mr. Lorenz, look at this. This is a thesis on chemical preparations you wrote at the École Polytechnique in Paris. You even won a scholarship for it, didn't you?”

“Yes, sir, but what does that have to do with now? If you want my research results, you could have just invited me, instead of kidnapping me here and then talking about academia.”

Ivan wagged his finger. “This is not an invitation, but a demand. Mr. Lorenz, our Russian government sincerely invited you to take a position in Russia a while ago, but you did not reply to us. And after our investigation, your thesis was then provided to a Nazi company, helping them with a great deal of production activities.” A gunshot suddenly rang out in the distance, and Ivan also took out a pistol from his pocket and wiped it. “According to Russian law, any form of funding for Nazi activities is punishable by execution. But considering your talent, we have decided to give you another chance.”

title: A Better Life
desc:
Inside a military camp in Yekaterinburg, the Vympel troops were in full swing, carrying out a re-equipment activity. Through special foreign intelligence channels, Russia's elite troops had obtained the latest Kevlar body armor from American mercenary companies. Although these items were somewhat damaged during delivery, after sufficient bribery and collection, Russian military industry successfully reverse-engineered a harder and lighter body armor. To distinguish it, they named it the 'Yevgeny body armor.'

...

In the city of Samara, Russian residents were happily receiving newly distributed clothing and bedding from the state-run stores. According to the news announced by the store leaders, the country's civil industry department had recently made a major breakthrough in production. They had gained new inspiration from foreign clothing and had greatly improved the comfort of the produced goods. After trying on the new clothes themselves, the people found them to be a better fit and less scratchy than the old ones.

...

In Omsk, an American shoe factory was closing its doors. The factory owner, Richard, was fiercely arguing with an official from the Omsk Ministry of Foreign Affairs. As an enterprising businessman, he had traveled thousands of miles from America to Russia to open up this blue ocean market. At first, his gamble paid off. The loafers he sold were a huge hit here, and state-run stores started placing orders with him. But in less than a few months, a large number of counterfeits appeared on the market. He personally bought a few pairs, and the production quality of many of them was almost the same as his! He angrily protested to the government, but in the following months, no one paid him any attention. Orders became fewer and fewer. He finally couldn't take it anymore and decided to shut down the factory.

...

title: Adaptation
desc:
Pavlov leaped out of his dorm bed, quickly made his bunk, put on his work clothes, and looked in the mirror. He considered himself apolitical. After all, no matter who ran the factory, scientific production and rational assembly line management were essential. He had always been confident about this. Whether it was the Salon or those warlords who came here, after consulting with the local workers, they all came to him respectfully, seeking his opinion and asking him to continue working. Pavlov himself was not stupid; he took every task seriously, so no one gave him much trouble.

Although recent days had been a bit chaotic—gunshots could be heard outside the factory from time to time in the morning, and the footsteps of soldiers running around could be heard in the afternoon, which annoyed many workers and affected their work. Fortunately, everyone was experienced and still managed to complete production on time and with quality. Thank God, Pavlov only hoped that whoever was outside could calm down and not disrupt production anymore. If this continued, he didn't want any more trouble for himself.

But unfortunately, trouble still found him. Before Pavlov could even start work, two soldiers summoned him to an office—the office where the former leader had been stationed. Inside sat a man in black. He glanced at Pavlov and then said,

“Mr. Pavlov, an order has come down from above. Our factory needs to undergo a comprehensive system reform recently. The details are extensive, and you will need to lead the workers to seriously study and adapt. Here is a study notebook, you can take a look first.”

Pavlov took the small booklet. The first thing that caught his eye was the so-called 'Omsk Experience.' He flipped through a few pages, his brows furrowing tighter and tighter. After reading a few pages, he couldn't help but ask worriedly: “Sir, is this really appropriate?”

“Why wouldn't it be?”

“You see, this so-called experience requires the workers to work almost around the clock. But our factory's workers already work more than ten hours in a row. Their spirits are exhausted every day. And this is with our factory's relatively good working conditions and timely payment of wages. If we increase the working hours, I'm worried the workers' rest will be severely affected.”

The leader waved his hand impatiently. “That's true, but you need to know that the country is about to face an unprecedented war. The Nazis are about to attack. If the workers can't even overcome this small difficulty, they will become the slaves of the Germans.”

“Then at least we should improve the working environment in the factory. With better conditions, the workers can at least rest after work. With good rest, they can produce more efficiently.”

“Comrade Pavlov, your thinking is very dangerous.” The leader in front of him stared at him. “Regarding this kind of thinking, the headquarters has a special summary: Productivism! This revisionist thinking only focuses on improving productivity, but is unwilling to mobilize the workers' enthusiasm! I see now, the reason your factory's productivity isn't increasing is because you lack ideological progress and study, only focusing on improving various conditions, but unwilling to produce more for the country. You have been slacking for too long, and we need to correct you!”

Pavlov had a thousand words flash through his mind. He wanted to say something, but couldn't get it out. Thinking of his wife at home, and his two hungry children, he finally bowed his head.

title: Full-Scale Operation
desc:
“The resources of Siberia are providing precious funds for the Great Trial. The League's army will continue to advance towards a more modern and elite goal!” Vladimir Starovsky was proclaiming his grand words to the Commander-in-Chief of the Great Trial.

“Good. You have indeed made a significant contribution to the Great Trial, a contribution I cannot simply summarize. But I think you should have a clear account for yourself.” Yazov's eyes cast a solemn and serious gaze at Starovsky. “How many billions of US dollars in revenue exactly? The funds needed for the Great Trial are far greater than we imagined.”

“Commander-in-Chief, as the head of the League's foreign trade statistics bureau, I naturally have a clear account of the revenue. The figure is 1.999B US dollars. I think this will not only provide a powerful impetus for the Great Trial, but there will even be money left over to improve the living conditions of the operatives, such as purchasing some…”

“Stop! Immediately cease your erroneous judgment and hedonism!” Yazov's face gradually darkened, turning to anger at the mention of the word 'purchase.' “The funds for the Great Trial are not for you to squander like that!”

Starovsky was first taken aback, but after a mental struggle, he still managed to stammer out, “Commander-in-Chief, I think the operatives are currently under great pressure, we should relax a little…”

Yazov angrily drove him out.

title: “Ground to Dust”
desc:
Grigory was the deputy chief of the police station in the city of Kostroma. Normally, in a country like the Black League, this position would be one of great prestige. However, now, two uninvited guests had barged into his office and pressed a pistol to his forehead.

A cold sweat instantly broke out on Grigory's brow. In that moment, many thoughts flashed through his mind: “What are the guards doing? Are they sleeping on the job? Has my secret been exposed?” But before he could think further, the man had already placed his finger on the trigger: “I ask, you answer. One extra word and I'll shoot you right now. Where is the next rendezvous point for your dirty dealings with the Germans? What are the codes and communication methods?”

His mind went blank in an instant, and he subconsciously asked: “How did you—”

“Shut the fuck up and stop wasting time!”

“Okay, okay, I, I'll talk. I agreed to meet them at the Yarahi Hotel, in two weeks, at eleven o'clock at night. They contact me through a collaborator for a one-way meeting. I don't know the collaborator's specific identity. But please don't kill me, I can gather intelligence for the League—”

A gunshot rang out, and his words were silenced.

The high-nosed agent picked up a walkie-talkie and reported to the person on the other end: “The intelligence sent back by our agents in Germany is correct. The crime of Grigory Vladimirovich Smirnov, deputy chief of the police station in the Kostromskoy district of Kostroma, colluding with the German beasts and selling out Russian intelligence has been verified. The criminal has been executed on the spot. Requesting instructions on how to handle his family.”

“Operative 602319, Operative 8039642, you have done well. Handle his family in the same way as you would any other traitor.” He paused for a moment, then said:

title: The Drill
desc:
Tatyana confidently glanced at her colleagues, then turned her attention back to the exercise unfolding on the after-action review map. This exercise was one of the new military requirements proposed by the Commander-in-Chief after approving a new round of military funding. The notice issued from above informed everyone that in order to allow the Russian army to adapt to more complex environments and longer combat durations, the military had provided the participating troops with higher equipment standards, but they also needed to adapt to more complex battlefield conditions. To get the troops up to speed for combat more quickly, the military had launched this large-scale exercise.

First was Tatyana's side. The radio in front of her was the first to buzz: “Sir, my unit encountered a nuclear radiation zone during the march. The chemical defense troops are responding in a timely manner. Please provide further instructions.”

“Pass through the radiation zone quickly. All units, please maintain contact. You must reach the designated area within the planned time, build fortifications, and launch a timely counter-attack.” Tatyana issued the order to every commander. The ample communication devices on the front line allowed Tatyana's orders to be relayed from mid-level officers to non-commissioned officers. After thorough preparation, her unit passed through the nuclear radiation zone in ten minutes. Although the exercise command still declared two-tenths of her heavy firepower equipment destroyed, her unit still quickly defeated an attacking guerrilla force after passing through and established a position at the designated location.

As for the other units, they were not so lucky. Some exercise units had twice the number of troops as Tatyana's, but due to untimely reporting, the exercise command directly declared more than half of them wiped out. Some units were even declared out of the exercise. The command post of a famous hero unit was taken out by guerrillas after passing through... As for the loss of heavy firepower equipment, it was countless.

If this was just the first appetizer, the following content of the exercise was even more difficult. After Tatyana's unit arrived, her unit first began to engage an enemy force several times its size. Airplanes, heavy artillery, and even chemical weapons were used in turn. But due to good battlefield communication construction, Tatyana's unit repulsed the enemy force with continuous artillery support. And through the electronic eavesdropping unit added before the exercise, they received intelligence that the so-called support force was actually a traitorous army. Before this unit arrived, they quickly shelled it, annihilating the traitors.

...

The results of the after-action review were quickly compiled into a text and disseminated to every unit in the Russian army through the military newspaper. And after reading the entire review, Yazov excitedly wrote an annotation:

The current budget is sufficient for the relevant project construction, and most of the necessary procurement items can be carried out in parallel with the planning of underground routes and factory air defense projects. If the project scale needs to be further expanded, please submit a timely application to the Ministry of National Development.

Project Items: In progress

Including but not limited to: anti-aircraft weapon configuration for major factories in various regions, internal protective unit partition walls in factories, design standards will be benchmarked against large anti-aircraft bombs; internal passage design must have clean areas, contaminated areas, and related sealed partition walls. If construction is completed, chemical agents can be deployed in specific locations for protection testing. ...

Construction Test Results: Good

Although our country currently lacks sufficient satellite equipment for space observation, through multiple rounds of irregular aircraft aerial photography tests, it can be concluded that the pilot bunkers in operation already possess strong anti-aircraft and anti-reconnaissance capabilities. Unless spy planes fly at extremely low altitudes and use ultra-high-density reconnaissance equipment, it is difficult to detect anything.

Intelligence Department Supplement: In recent years, the Nazi research institute has proposed the development of a bunker-buster bomb, which could cause great damage to our underground facilities. It is hoped that the design department will carry out deep reinforcement in response to this.

...

In summary, Project Chameleon is ready to begin construction.

title: Rekindled
desc:
What should I do?

Whenever asked this question, Shtemenko would either remain silent or talk around the subject. The question was too difficult for him to answer, just as no one could accurately predict the future direction of the Russian land. One turn of events after another occurred in Shtemenko's life of nearly 50 years, turning him from a forward-charging hothead into a silent bystander.

Before the outbreak of the Great Patriotic War, he was an ordinary worker in the Central Siberian region. After graduating from high school, he entered an aircraft factory and learned from outstanding designers like Lavochkin. After the war broke out, Shtemenko joined the party and the army. He was confident that through hard work and production, he could defeat the Nazi invaders. But the collapse of Bukharin's Soviet Union dealt him a severe blow. At first, he thought of going to Tyumen to find the Soviet government, but the local salons and factory owners suddenly declared that the Soviets were no longer needed here, and that he was a glorious citizen of the Central Siberian Republic. Shtemenko could have accepted this, but when these scholars asked him to fire on his former comrades-in-arms, Shtemenko finally could not accept it and retired home.

Over a dozen years passed. Shtemenko witnessed great changes. Russians killed each other for all sorts of different -isms, and some were even unwilling to provoke the Germans, letting the motherland's territory be occupied. Shtemenko had nothing to say about this, as long as they didn't surrender to the Germans.

Finally, Russia was unified. The unifiers were a group of soldiers in black. After conducting a population census here for a few months, they found Shtemenko. The leading officer drank with him all night, talking about how he had followed the army west to try to restore the motherland, only to be betrayed by traitors from within and defeated by the Nazis. To avenge himself on the Germans, he followed Commander Karbyshev and Commander-in-Chief Yazov, two true great men who did everything they could for the motherland's revenge on the Nazis. After that night, Shtemenko returned to the design bureau, serving as a senior technician.

“The data needs to be more precise, there can't be any errors in the welding here, it will cause problems with our aircraft.” Shtemenko stood beside a worker, guiding him in a gentle tone. He now understood that from the very beginning, he had never given up on one obsession, one opportunity to eliminate the Nazi invaders and win a bit of face for himself and his country.

title: Different Views
desc:
“…Hey, young man, don't go over there. That's where the Salvation Brigade works. They're just a bunch of the motherland's garbage. The work they do is the heaviest, the most life-threatening. If you go over there looking for them, you'll have a hard time.”

“Thank you, uncle. Are you also a volunteer here to build the motherland's power grid?”

“Me? I'm not a volunteer. I'm just cannon fodder for the motherland. When the motherland needs me, I have to come out and work. If I can survive this job, I might be able to get a spot in the regular army in the future?”

“Uncle, is the treatment in the League's regular army very good?”

“(Looks around, lowers his voice) The treatment is a little better than those garbage in the Salvation Brigade, but not by much. The main thing is that ordinary people won't dare to mess with you anymore. If anyone messes with you, they'll get a bullet.”

“So how did you end up working here, uncle?”

“I didn't offend the League, I offended the League's previous regime. I was thrown in prison, and it was the League's people who let me out. But they also said that people like me have sinned against Russia, and I still need to atone for Russia.”

“Aren't you a good person? What sin do you have to atone for?”

“Sigh, the foreman isn't here, I'll be straight with you. I'm just afraid of dying. These black-clothed men of the League talk every day about dedicating everything to the motherland, but this dedication often means your life. Digging in the mines until you die, working overtime until you die, and so on. But I don't want to die. I just want to earn some money, marry a wife, and be able to afford two bottles of vodka a day.”

“Aren't you afraid I'll report you?”

“If you want to, go ahead. You're a good young man, you have your own conscience. You're so young, don't end up like us garbage, rotting away on this construction site. You should go to those big cities. The future of the motherland needs people like you to build.”

“No, uncle. This is my home, after all. Once we have electricity, our people's lives will be better in the future. We won't be living in grime forever.”

title: Site 27, Part One
desc:
Even after several years, though eroded by wind and sand, little here had changed.

Wind whipped sand against the armored vehicle's bulletproof glass, making a fine, cracking sound. Colonel Konstantin observed the horizon's silhouette through his binoculars—behind the collapsed walls, a few concrete buildings stood crookedly, the glass of most towers completely shattered.

"Radiation levels?" the Colonel's voice was muffled by his gas mask.

Technician Ivanovich tapped the dashboard: "0.18 millisieverts, Colonel. Lower than expected." The instrument's glass reflected the sunlight, casting a spiderweb of light on his face.

Konstantin nodded and strode forward. His boot soles crunched on broken glass and rusted bolts. The guide, Alim, followed behind him, his gaze warily scanning every shadow. His father had once been an engineer here.

The main building's door had long rusted shut. The soldiers forced it open with hydraulic pliers. Dust floated in the sunlight, illuminating the empty corridor. Yellowed documents were scattered on the floor. Konstantin bent down and picked one up—an experiment log, dated 1969, the last line reading: "Reactor cooling system failure, emergency shutdown."

"Looks like it was an accident," Viktor said, kicking a loose piece of wall. "But maybe we'll find something yet."

They continued deeper, through abandoned laboratories. The equipment was long since powered down, control panels covered in dust, the glass of the meters shattered, their needles frozen in time. Alim stood before an iron door, hesitating.

"This is the second basement level," he said in a low voice. "My father said... they tested some kind of new reactor here."

Konstantin pushed the iron door open, his flashlight beam sweeping through the darkness. In the center of the room was a huge cylindrical device, its shell covered in rivets and welds, surrounded by lead suits and detection instruments. Fortunately, there was no abnormal radiation, only the signs of time's erosion.

"Abandoned experimental equipment," Konstantin approached, his fingertips brushing against the metal surface, the cold touch like that of the Siberian permafrost.

"Colonel!" Viktor found an old terminal in the corner. The screen had long since gone dark, but the drawer next to it was stuffed with a stack of documents. Konstantin opened the topmost one—"Site 27 Final Report," stamped with "Top Secret."

He quickly scanned a few pages, his brow gradually relaxing.

"The place was sealed after the reactor experiment failed," he closed the document. "Nothing abnormal. At least that fellow Fyodor didn't mess things up too badly."

"So... what do we do next?" Viktor asked.

Konstantin looked around, his gaze sweeping over the mottled walls, rusted pipes, and silent machines.

"Rebuild," he said curtly. "The Black League needs this base."

As they walked out of the main building, the sun was sinking below the horizon, dyeing the wasteland a dark red. Konstantin stood on the steps, gazing at the sprawling desert, as if something had come to mind...

"Begin cleanup tomorrow," he ordered.

title: Dusk Falls—For the Commander-in-Chief's Eyes Only
desc:
To: Commander-in-Chief Yazov
From: Shevchenko Reconstruction Committee, Colonel Konstantin Antonovich

Commander-in-Chief Comrade:
Following an on-site inspection, the main structure of the experimental facilities at Site 27 remains intact. The reactor chamber on the second basement level and its auxiliary equipment have not suffered severe damage. Although the surface buildings show signs of weathering, the core experimental area (including the main reactor vessel, cooling system, and control terminals) still has the potential for basic functional restoration. Radiation levels are generally stable within safe thresholds, with no risk of contamination spread. It is recommended to prioritize the repair of the power supply and ventilation systems for subsequent in-depth assessment.
This facility once undertook testing of the Kazakh nuclear reactor prototype and nuclear weapons. Although neither was successful, their design concepts remain valuable for reference today. The technical documents left on site (including the 'Site 27 Final Report') indicate that the project had achieved milestone breakthroughs before the accident. If its data can be decrypted, it may provide key technological nodes for the Black League's nuclear weapons program. Furthermore, the complete underground bunker structure, with minor modifications, can be used as a strategic reserve base.
Based on the on-site exploration, it is recommended that the reconstruction project proceed in three phases: basic reinforcement and environmental purification; key equipment repair and data recovery; modernization and functional expansion. A team of nuclear engineering experts needs to be dispatched to take up residence, focusing on cracking the reactor's safety redundancy design. According to the accompanying experts' predictions, it will only take three months to have most of the facilities safely re-enabled and put into research and development, and six months to have all facilities fully repaired. In addition, restarting these facilities will save 70% of the cost of building a new base, and will provide a pivot point for the nuclear weapons layout of the Black in Central Asia and the progress of the Black League's nuclear weapons research and development.
Considering that Project 416's test site is in Semipalatinsk, Fort Shevchenko will also need to establish a complete set of transportation facilities to transport nuclear weapons and heavy equipment to the Semipalatinsk test site.
In accordance with General Order GL-0014, all non-Black League members involved in this reconnaissance operation have been executed.
The Great Trial will come.

title: Site 27, Part Two
desc:
An iron-grey mist shrouded Fort Shevchenko before dawn. The tall cooling towers were faint silhouettes in the morning light, and newly welded steel frames reflected the cold gleam. Workers dragged their weary feet through the checkpoint, their boots leaving blurred footprints on the not-yet-dry concrete.

"Heard B-sector's reactor is going to test run next week," Igor whispered, nudging Vasily with his shoulder.

Vasily didn't answer immediately. His gaze swept over the Black League soldiers patrolling nearby. The gas-masked figures were like faceless ghosts in the mist. Only when the soldiers' footsteps faded did he pull a crumpled half-cigarette from his pocket.

"Test run?" he sneered, cupping his hands against the wind to light it. "Last month they said D-sector's safety system was debugged. Three days later, they carried out four bodies."

Igor subconsciously touched the radiation badge on his left arm—a small black device every worker was forced to wear before entering the core area.

The low hum of machinery came from the mist. On the east side of the base, workers queued for breakfast—black bread hard as a rock and a bowl of thin soup with a few floating vegetable leaves. The cafeteria walls were covered with new propaganda posters, printed with the Black League's double-headed eagle and a line of bright red text: "Contribute to the glorious future of the Motherland!"

"My daughter wrote last week," old welder Sergei suddenly spoke, his rough fingers caressing a photo hidden in his work clothes pocket. "She said the Black League gave the families medals... said we were doing glorious work."

The table fell silent. Andrei, an apprentice electrician not yet twenty, stared at his distorted reflection in the soup bowl. Three months ago when he was conscripted, propaganda vans in his hometown square posted photos of Fort Shevchenko—the sun was bright in the pictures, and the workers smiled and waved goodbye to their families.

"At least..." Igor broke the silence, "at least we can send money home every month."

A harsh whistle interrupted the conversation. The soldiers began to urge the workers to line up. The voice behind the gas mask, electronically processed, was an emotionless mechanical sound: "A-sector, team three, proceed immediately to A-sector corridor. Repeat, proceed immediately to A-sector corridor."

They came to the newly laid A-sector corridor. The LED lights on the ceiling emitted a harsh blue light. The surveillance cameras on both sides of the corridor slowly turned with their movement. The door to A-sector was new, the heavy lead plate stamped with the prominent Black League logo.

"Wiring check," the foreman handed each of them a blueprint. The dense wiring diagrams made Andrei's head spin. "Must be finished before lunch."

As they crouched behind the control console, wiring, Vasily suddenly grabbed Andrei's wrist. On the young man's arm, the edge of the radiation badge was faintly glowing an unnatural blue.

"Don't look," Vasily said in a voice only they could hear. "And don't tell anyone."

Outside the window, the first ray of sunlight finally pierced the mist, shining on the repaired reactor casing in the center of the base. The new metal surface gleamed, like a newly polished coffin. Further away, a new team of workers was getting off a transport truck. They looked around blankly, just like Andrei three months ago.

When the lunch whistle blew again, no one mentioned the letters from their families. They silently chewed their food, listening to the league's declaration playing on a loop from the broadcast: "...under the guidance of Yazov…”

title: Midnight Nears—For the Commander-in-Chief's Eyes Only
desc:
To: Commander-in-Chief Yazov
From: Shevchenko Reconstruction Committee, Colonel Konstantin Antonovich


Commander-in-Chief Comrade:

As of this month, the first phase of the Fort Shevchenko military nuclear facility reconstruction project has been successfully completed, with 85% of the main facilities restored to operational capacity. The A-sector reactor has been rebuilt, but the previous design proved unable to make the reactor operate effectively. The main control system has been rebuilt, the reactor building's structure has been reinforced, and the updating of the main control room equipment is proceeding in an orderly manner. All engineering personnel are working efficiently under military control, ensuring the rapid recovery of this strategic location. The data required by the Semipalatinsk test site and nuclear research institute has been compiled and will be delivered in its entirety in three days.

Several technical difficulties still remain in the engineering process. The radiation shielding system in the test site area requires a professional team for final debugging. The reactor will be redesigned. Considering the special status of this facility in the Black League's nuclear deterrent system, the current lack of technical strength may affect subsequent strategic deployment. It is recommended to immediately transfer a special working group of senior experts from the nuclear research institute, and at the same time, dispatch strictly vetted technical engineering troops to participate in the construction of key links.

Considering that the construction personnel will pose a serious leak risk to Black League secrets. In accordance with General Order GL-0014, it is requested that after the completion of the Fort Shevchenko reconstruction project, all worker groups be executed in batches under the name of 'glorious sacrifice.' This will not only eliminate the risk of leaks, but also create a sterile environment for subsequent sensitive experiments.

I implore the Commander-in-Chief to approve special operational authority.

The Great Trial will come.

title: Site 27, Part Three
desc:
A cold wind swept fine snow across the newly paved square of Fort Shevchenko. The concrete buildings gleamed coldly under the lead-grey sky. Vasily stood in the ranks, gazing at the nuclear facility they had rebuilt with their own hands—the huge reactor casing polished to a mirror shine, the white steam from the ventilation towers twisting and dissipating in the cold wind. In just six months, they had poured their sweat onto this barren land, turning a ruin into an iron fortress by a miracle.

"Everyone, assemble in the main hall!" the officer's voice came through the loudspeaker, cold and mechanical. "The completion ceremony is about to begin."

The workers dragged their weary feet towards the central building, their boots crunching on the thin snow. Vasily noticed that there were twice as many guards as usual today. The soldiers were fully armed, their eyes behind the gas masks as cold as machines. The main hall's doors were open, brightly lit inside. There was even vodka and black bread on the long tables—a rare luxury.

"Finally going home..." the young electrician Mikhail whispered, his eyes sparkling with anticipation.

Vasily didn't answer. His gaze swept over the hall—every exit was guarded by armed soldiers, and on the second-floor corridor, the silhouettes of snipers were faintly visible. His stomach suddenly tightened, a familiar fear crawling up his spine—the same feeling he had when he first set foot on this wasteland three years ago.

The officer stood on the stage, expressionlessly reading a document: "...thank you all for your contribution to the great cause of the Black League..."

"What does that mean?" a gruff voice suddenly interrupted him. Old welder Grigory pushed through the crowd, the icicles on his beard trembling with his excited breath. "What about our families? The promised bonuses?"

The hall fell silent. The soldiers' muzzles lifted slightly.

The officer continued to read: "...all workers who participated in the Fort Shevchenko reconstruction project will receive... special placement..."

"Liar!" Mikhail suddenly screamed, his voice echoing in the empty hall. "You never intended to let us leave!"

Countless fragments of memory suddenly flashed before Vasily's eyes—the desolate towers when he first arrived, the pain of tightening bolts with frozen fingers, the letters he secretly wrote to his daughter at night but could never send... and the disappeared co-workers, the ones who were dragged away by the soldiers and never returned.

"Get them!" Grigory roared, grabbing a bottle of vodka.

The gunshots rang out almost at the same time.

Vasily felt a sharp pain. He looked down and saw the flower of blood blooming on his chest. In the moment he fell, he saw his friends: Andrei, Igor, Sergei… their eyes gradually emptied, finally losing their light. He seemed to see his daughter's smile again—the little girl who was only five when he left home, she should know how to write the alphabet by now, right?

As the last bullet pierced his temple, Vasily vaguely heard the officer's cold voice: "Clean it up, I don't want to see them again tomorrow."

title: The Midnight Bell Tolls—For the Commander-in-Chief's Eyes Only
desc:
To: Commander-in-Chief Yazov
From: Shevchenko Reconstruction Committee, Colonel Konstantin Antonovich


Commander-in-Chief Comrade:

The reconstruction of the Fort Shevchenko strategic nuclear facility has been successfully completed according to plan. All systems have been restored to optimal operational status. The reactor and its control facilities have undergone comprehensive debugging and are now formally in use, fully meeting the strategic deterrence needs of the Black League. All personnel involved in the construction have been subjected to the final disposal procedure in accordance with the highest secrecy regulations, ensuring that project details will not be leaked. The entire process proceeded without any unforeseen incidents, with all stages progressing smoothly according to the established plan.

Considering the extreme sensitivity of this project, it is recommended to implement preventive measures against the relatives of some workers who may have been exposed to sensitive information. Although these families have not been formally investigated, according to the preliminary assessment of relevant departments, there is a potential risk of leaks. To completely eliminate this hidden danger, in accordance with General Order GL-0014, authorization is now requested to directly execute a special operation without going through the regular review process. This will maximize the strategic security of Fort Shevchenko and ensure that the core interests of the Black League are not threatened.

I implore the Commander-in-Chief to approve special operational authority.

The Great Trial will come.

title: Site 27, Part Four
desc:
Vasily's daughter, Alyona, stood on tiptoe, hanging the last paper crane on the string in front of the window. There were nearly two hundred she had prepared for her father—a sentence was hidden in the wings of each crane. When Papa came back, she would unfold them one by one for him to hear.

"Mama, has Papa's letter arrived?" Alyona turned and asked, her blue eyes dancing with the firelight.

Marina stopped kneading the dough, wiping the flour on her apron. "Soon," she said with a smile, but her voice was as tight as a bowstring. "The last letter said the project was almost finished."

Marina would stop whatever she was doing every day when the postman passed, and had not missed once in six months. The other families in the village involved in the 'special national project' did the same—they shared the thin letters stamped with the black eagle, trying to decipher a few words from the almost identical,潦草 (liáocǎo - cursive/hasty) handwriting.

Until this morning, the postman's bell rang more urgently than usual.

When Marina took the gilt-edged envelope, her fingers suddenly wouldn't obey. The envelope was too thick, not like the usual paper-saving letters 'Vasily' wrote. She excitedly tore open the wax seal, and a photograph slid out—Vasily in a military dress uniform she had never seen before, a medal gleaming strangely on his chest.

The words 'martyr' and 'glorious sacrifice' on the official paper stabbed into her eyes like blades. Marina's voice suddenly shattered. The teapot on the stove let out a sharp whistle, just like the train whistle when Vasily left home six months ago.

Alyona didn't yet understand what 'sacrifice' meant, but she saw her mother's tears fall on her father's photograph, blurring the medal into a vague golden puddle.

Late at night, Marina still couldn't sleep, memories of her time with Vasily flooding back. From their shy first meeting to later having a daughter—life had been so sweet, so beautiful. Even though the world outside was burning, their careful nurturing had kept this little family safe from harm. And then, Vasily was conscripted for a secret project…

Suddenly, all the lights in the building went out at once, and the roar of an engine came from outside. Marina rushed to the window and saw two black cars crushing her carefully tended vegetable garden. Figures in uniforms were checking the house numbers, as if looking for a particular family.

When Alyona was awakened, Marina was holding her and her cookie tin in the cellar.

"Mama, who are they?" Alyona asked, clutching the paper crane. When the sound of a gun bolt being pulled came from outside, Marina stuffed the paper crane into her daughter's inner pocket and kissed her forehead one last time: "Alyona, remember, your papa built the strongest house in the world..."

A gunshot rang out, followed by another, and another…

As the car drove away from the burning farmhouse, a paper crane floated out of the window, carried by the heatwave into the starry sky. The tender pencil writing on the paper was gradually consumed by the flames:

title: The Annihilation of Central Asia—For the Commander-in-Chief's Eyes Only
desc:
To: Commander-in-Chief Yazov
From: Ministry of Internal Affairs, Minister Yuri Drozdov


Commander-in-Chief Comrade:

Following the oil crisis and the Turkic Congress, the Central Asian region is currently in an unprecedented power vacuum. Local government institutions are nearly paralyzed, public discontent continues to ferment, and the entire region is on the brink of total insurrection. Our intelligence network on the ground confirms that anti-government demonstrations have erupted in several key cities, and the original forces of order have lost control of the situation. This chaotic state of affairs provides an excellent opportunity for the League to implement strategic expansion—Central Asia's rich energy reserves and key geographical location will greatly enhance the Black League's control over the Eurasian continent. Considering that other nations are currently preoccupied, this is the golden window for us to march south and seize control of this Eurasian artery in one fell swoop.

To ensure the long-term stability of the Central Asian region after the war, it is recommended to immediately launch the 'Purifying Dawn' plan after the military operation is concluded, to carry out the necessary 'population restructuring' in strategic nodal cities (see encrypted appendix 1). Historical lessons show that these regions have always been breeding grounds for resistance forces. Only through decisive special measures can the sources of instability be eradicated at their root. It is requested to grant the frontline commanders full discretionary authority, allowing them to implement undisclosed management measures against specific populations according to the actual situation, without going through cumbersome judicial procedures. This will effectively deter potential opposition forces and lay the foundation for the subsequent establishment of permanent military control.

I implore the Commander-in-Chief to approve special operational authority.

The Great Trial will come.

title: A Gift
desc:
The morning mist had not yet dispersed over Pavlodar's central square, and the bronze statue of the 'Russo-Kazakh Friendship' monument was a faint silhouette in the fog. The bullet holes on the statue's base were like ugly scars, and the remaining inscriptions were covered with splattered mud. Sasha's red, frozen fingers touched the crumpled leaflet in his pocket. The ink of 'Bread and Work' had already bled.

"They wouldn't dare to shoot," old Ivan muttered ahead, a few strands of grey-white hair showing from under his sheepskin hat. "We just want something to eat."

The crowd surged towards the city hall square like a muddy river. Sasha saw women holding babies, old soldiers leaning on crutches, workers in faded overalls—all with the same numb anger on their faces. Last week, when the Black League's tanks rolled over the frozen Irtysh River, the radio said it was a 'liberation,' but the price of bread in the grain store had tripled.

"Liars!" a young girl in a red scarf suddenly shouted, jumping onto the broken edge of the fountain. The water had long since dried up, the bottom covered in blackened snow. "My father worked at the machine tool factory for forty years, now even his pension—"

The shriek of a loudspeaker cut her off. A few black-uniformed figures appeared on the city hall balcony, the lenses of their gas masks reflecting the cold morning light.

"Please do not disturb public order..." a mechanized voice echoed across the square. "Disperse immediately, or necessary measures will be taken."

The crowd grew restless. Sasha heard someone behind him spit: "Necessary measures? Like last month in the workers' dormitories? Is that how you treat your own fucking countrymen?!"

Old Ivan suddenly held up a piece of black bread as hard as a rock: "Is this the gift you give to the people?" His cold smile trembled in the wind. "The Tsar in 1912 was more merciful than you!"

When the first shot rang out, Sasha thought it was firecrackers. It wasn't until old Ivan's sheepskin hat flew off, revealing a bloody, mangled half-head, that he realized it was no joke. The square erupted in an instant. Amidst screams and curses, more gunshots came from all directions.

"Get down!" the girl in the red scarf dragged Sasha into the dry fountain pool. Bullets struck the bronze statue, sparking brightly. Sasha saw the officer who had been shouting, gesturing with his leather-gloved hand, as if conducting a symphony.

On the other side of the fountain, a man in overalls suddenly stood up, raising his hands: "We just want—"

Three bullets struck his chest simultaneously. As the man fell, a photo fluttered from his pocket and landed in front of Sasha—it was an old group photo from the machine tool factory, the incomplete slogan 'Siberian Plan' still clearly visible in the background.

When the roar of armored vehicles drowned out the cries, Sasha found himself laughing. How ironic. This city had witnessed the friendship of two peoples, and now that friendship had turned into lead and blood. The red-scarfed girl gripped his arm tightly, her nails digging into his flesh: "Kazakhstan..."

Her next words were swallowed by an explosion. And this scene was replaying itself on every street and alley of Pavlodar, while their compatriots remained completely unaware of the impending atrocity.

And in a military base two hundred kilometers away, a Black League officer was drawing red circles on a map:

title: What Awaits Akmola…
desc:
The evening sun's fading rays cast a golden hue on the cobblestone streets of the old bazaar, gilding the ancient market. Anton Ivanovich, carrying a worn leather briefcase, stopped at Uncle Sergei's fruit stand. The sweet aroma of ripe fruit mixed with the scent of cinnamon from the nearby spice stall drifted through the air.

"Old friend, pick me some of the sweetest apples," Anton said with a smile, taking off his hat to reveal his slightly graying temples. "Today is a special day."

Uncle Sergei looked up from behind a wooden crate, his white beard trembling with his smile: "Ah, Anton! I knew you'd come today." The old man's rough fingers deftly moved among a row of apples. "Little Ivan's birthday today, right? Six years old? Time flies, it really does. When I first saw that cute little fellow, he wasn't even as tall as the counter…" Sergei placed his hand on the row of crates, trying to show little Ivan's former height.

"Yes, this child, he'll be starting school in a flash." Anton's gaze softened, watching the old man carefully select the fruit. "Natasha baked his favorite honey cake, and I promised to help decorate it after work."

The stall owner packed three rosy, plump apples into a paper bag, then added a few golden apricots: "These apricots are very sweet, a gift from me to the little one." He lowered his voice, "They just arrived yesterday, didn't go through the rationing station, fresh."

Anton nodded gratefully, and carefully took a small box from his briefcase: "I bought him this, a small train model, just like the freight locomotive I drive. The little one always looks at me with longing eyes when I go to work..."

"He's going to be ecstatic!" Uncle Sergei's eyes narrowed into a slit. "My grandson Alexei is always talking about playing with him. Last time they were at the park…"

The old man's words suddenly froze in the air. Anton felt a warm liquid splash on his face. He stared blankly as Uncle Sergei's chest was rapidly stained red. The paper bag full of fruit slipped from the old man's hand, the apples rolling onto the cobblestones with a dull thud.

Time seemed to slow down to an crawl. Anton saw Uncle Sergei's lips still moving, but no sound came out; saw the big auntie at the next spice stall turn her head in astonishment, the cinnamon powder in her hand tracing a strange golden arc in the air; saw old Sergei's grandson Alexei peeking out from behind the stall, still holding the wooden toy he was going to give to Ivan.

Then, the world started moving again.

Anton staggered back a step, his briefcase falling to the ground, its contents scattering. He subconsciously reached for his chest, his fingers touching the box with the little train model. In the distance, a few black figures were silently putting away their weapons and turning to leave, as if they had just completed a routine task.

On the cobblestones, the apples Anton had bought for his son lay quietly in a pool of blood. The setting sun's rays, passing through the fruit's skin, made it look like a beating heart.

Uncle Sergei had fallen onto his fruit stand, one hand still reaching for the apricot he was going to give to little Ivan. In the last moments of his life, Anton could still see the lingering smile in the old man's eyes…

As dusk fell, the lights of the bazaar would never be lit again. And on the other side of the city, in an ordinary apartment, Natasha was placing the last candle on a honey cake, while little Ivan knelt by the window, waiting for his father to bring home the birthday apples…

title: The “Rose's” Diary
desc:
Date: (crossed out) Weather: (crossed out)

Almaty is burning.

I gaze at the rising smoke in the distance, my fingers, stained with a mixture of ink and tears, trembling on this diary that will soon go to my grave. This city of apples, nourished by the snowmelt of the Tian Shan for a thousand years, this pearl of the Silk Road that once made Persian caravans stop in awe, is now having its spine crushed by the treads of the Black League.

I vaguely remember my childhood, when my father took me to the Zenkov Cathedral in the old city. Sunlight, passing through the stained glass windows, cast rainbows on the stone slabs. Then, the sound of the cathedral bells and the mosque's call to prayer resonated in harmony. Russian children and Kazakh youths chased the tram together on Turkestan Avenue. When the railway opened, the whole city trembled with the roar of the steam locomotive—it was a tremor of hope. We naively believed that the railway would bring prosperity to the autonomous region…

But what the railway brought was the Soviet NKVD that poisoned the motherland, and this horrifying group of black executioners. When I was a guide at the Central State Museum, I once caressed the sheepskin map from the era of Abylai Khan. The migration routes of the nomadic tribes were like the blood vessels of the earth. Now, these ignorant fools have replaced the ancient artifacts in the museum's glass cases with exhibition panels on the "glorious history of the great League," while true history is turning to ash in the book-burning furnaces…

My pen is running out of ink, just as the life of this city is coming to an end. The hustle and bustle of the market, the laughter of children, the chime of ancient bells, have all turned into the sound of armored vehicles crushing the road outside my window, interspersed with sporadic gunshots. The soul of my beloved motherland is burning, her marrow being devoured by the Black League—in the end, she will be reduced to ashes in the fire of an alien's revenge…

Almaty, my apple blossom, my snow-mountain rose. You have witnessed the camel caravans of the Seljuks, endured the iron hooves of the Dzungars, yet at the crossroads of modern civilization, you have been betrayed by the children you raised. When the Tsarist officers stripped you of your pastures with the 'Steppe Regulations,' when the Soviet commissars crushed your nomadic soul with collective farms, you still managed to preserve the embers in the dark. But now these executioners in their yellow and black armbands, they will even scatter the ashes into the Ili River.

Everything can finally end. I place the handwritten copy of the 'Book of Words of Abai,' which I have treasured for years, on top of this diary. It was a treasure my mother gave me on her deathbed, every page soaked in the true Kazakh soul. The noose is already tied, hanging from the oak bookshelf my father made for me.

Farewell, my motherland, whom I have never truly seen free. When spring finally comes to the foot of the Tian Shan, please let the melting snow carry away my ashes and nourish the roots of those scorched apple trees.

How I wish I could see you one last time…

title: The End of Another Riot
desc:
The morning mist had not yet dissipated, but Abay was already filling sacks with sand. His palms were blistered from the coarse hemp rope, but compared to the sound of cannon fire in the distance, this pain was nothing.

"Young man, take a rest," an old man selling naan stuffed a warm flatbread into his hand. "My grandson is about your age, studying in Almaty... I'm afraid now..."

Abay took the bread, not daring to ask further. Refugees who had fled from Almaty three days ago said the streets there were piled with bodies, even the mosques had not been spared. He looked towards the road, where machine parts from the factory, dismantled door panels, and even a few overturned trams were piled up—anything that could be used to block the tanks.

"I hear they don't even spare the children," said Mainur, the tailor, as she sewed white cloth strips onto sandbags, her voice low. Her husband had gone to the city outskirts with a hunting rifle yesterday and had not returned.

Abay wiped his sweat and continued to move sandbags. He was only seventeen this year, supposed to be an apprentice at the machine factory, but now he had to build this ridiculous defensive line with all the old people and women of the city. In the distance, a few retired veterans were teaching women how to use rifles, the crisp sound of bolts being pulled was particularly sharp in the morning mist.

"Look! It's the army!" someone suddenly shouted.

Abay looked up and saw a column of soldiers in uniform walking towards the city. At the very front was a one-armed old man, his chest covered in medals—it was Major Saken, who had been retired for years. The 'army' following him brought a lump to Abay's throat: the limping postman, the bespectacled teacher, the wrinkled shepherd... all holding a motley collection of weapons, from rusty hunting rifles to kitchen knives.

"Children," Major Saken's voice was hoarse but firm, "the beasts of the Black League are twenty kilometers away."

The crowd fell silent. Abay saw Mainur tie the white cloth strip around her forehead; it was clearly the material for a shroud.

"We have no tanks, no planes," the major raised his remaining right arm, "but we have every brick, every drop of blood in Shymkent!"

Someone started singing 'Wake up, Kazakhs,' and gradually, everyone joined in. Abay remembered his father's words before he died: "For decades, our nation has been fighting for its own destiny... Whether it was the Tsar or the Soviets, we never surrendered... Abay, you must remember: the Kazakh people can be defeated, but they will never surrender."

At noon, dust rose on the horizon.

"They're here!" the boy in the watchtower shouted.

Abay lay behind the sandbags, for the first time seeing the Black League's army clearly—dozens of tanks in a wedge formation, followed by an endless line of infantry. The sunlight reflected coldly off their gas masks.

When the first shell landed on the city gate, Abay was thrown to the ground by the blast wave. He got up and saw that half of Major Saken's body was gone, but the old man was still pointing forward with his remaining arm.

"For Kazakhstan!"

Someone shouted this slogan, and then, a miracle happened. The ragged crowd surged towards the iron tide like a wave. Abay saw Mainur charging at the front with a kitchen knife; the naan seller holding a homemade firebomb; even the university student who had fled from Almaty was waving an iron bar...

The second wave of artillery covered the charging crowd. A sharp pain shot through Abay's left leg, but he still struggled to crawl forward. Through the smoke, he saw the Black League soldiers reloading, their cold barrels aimed at the last batch of charging old people and children.

Abay stood up with all his might, holding up the national flag he had taken from someone's hand. In the instant the rain of bullets pierced his body, he seemed to see his father's smiling face… 

Then, he let out one last cry:

title: One Country, a Double Victory
desc:
As Colonel Ivan Kozlov's leather boots stepped over the broken glass of Frunze's central square, the setting sun was bathing the 'Victory Monument' in a blood-like light. He reached out and touched the not-yet-dry blood on the monument's base. The sticky sensation at his fingertips was like caressing a piece of rotten flesh.

"Is this what victors look like?" he asked the empty square, his voice echoing among the bullet-riddled buildings. Three days ago, the Kyrgyz were fighting the Black League army here. Now, only a few uncollected bodies remained, one of which still clutched a Kyrgyz flag, burned down to half its size.

Kozlov slowly walked towards the city hall, the hem of his greatcoat sweeping over the scattered leaflets on the road—these were self-printed by the resisters, their content quite chaotic. The city hall's bronze doors were twisted from an explosion, a severed hand stuck in the crack, a wedding ring on its ring finger reflecting a faint light.

"Colonel, you should see this," a lieutenant lifted the curtain to the basement, a hot, putrid stench rushing out. More than thirty 'resistance army' officials were crammed into this room, once used for storing archives, all executed in a kneeling position, the bullet holes in the back of their heads neatly aligned.

"They call this a strategic reserve," he kicked a moldy flour sack in the corner. "With this stuff, they thought they could compete with the Black League's army. What a pipe dream." Kozlov couldn't help but let out a cold laugh.

As night fell, Kozlov stood on the reviewing stand of the former Victory Square. Searchlights cast his shadow onto the walls of the opposite building, as huge as a demon. Sappers were placing explosives at the base of the monument, while his aide held a captured antique pocket watch and began the countdown.

"Ten, nine, eight…"

He thought of those scoundrels in the so-called 'camps' in the city's outskirts. They must be being covered by the Black League's artillery fire at this very moment. These mongrels must still think they can snatch back what they consider to be their Kyrgyz motherland's 'territory' from the enemy, just like a dozen years ago.

"...three, two, one!"

Amidst the deafening explosion, the thirty-meter-high monument slowly tilted. Kozlov watched as the inscriptions celebrating victory shattered in the firelight. Marble fragments crashed onto the square, crushing the unclaimed bodies once more.

"Report, Colonel, Frunze radio station is operational," the communications officer handed him a microphone.

Kozlov cleared his throat, his voice broadcasting from the city's remaining loudspeakers: "All Kyrgyz people in the city, whether you have surrendered or are still resisting…" he crushed a rotten head that had rolled to his feet, "...please abandon your foolishness. You have only one true motherland, and that is the Black League..."

After the smoke cleared, the newly erected Black League flag fluttered in the square. Kozlov took the vodka from his aide and raised a toast to this dead city: "To a double victory—we have destroyed your army, and you… have long since destroyed your own souls."
